title: Stigma and reducing prejudice

match.reason: The bank point defines stereotypes and prejudice and only briefly notes that getting to know someone helps, while the new point is about stigma and the conditions that reduce prejudice (equal-terms contact, shared goals, challenging stereotypes), so it is a related but different idea.

draft.title: Stigma and reducing prejudice
card: a mark of shame that society attaches to a person or group, such as for a mental illness. Stigma can lead people to be avoided or judged.
Prejudice, discrimination and stigma can harm wellbeing. They can cause stress, isolation and lower self-esteem, and can stop people seeking help.
Contact between groups can reduce prejudice when it is on equal terms, with neither group holding more status or power. Working toward a shared goal that needs everyone helps too.
Challenging stereotypes also helps. Learning accurate facts about a group, and meeting members who do not fit the stereotype, can change beliefs.
draft.remember: Equal contact, shared goals and challenged stereotypes can reduce prejudice.

a.q: Why can stigma harm a person's wellbeing?
opts: It can isolate them and stop them seeking help
It makes them more likely to be well known
It always changes their group's stereotype
It gives them equal status with other groups
a.why: Stigma can make a person feel ashamed and avoided, so they may withdraw or hide a problem instead of seeking help. It does not improve status or fix stereotypes.
a.clue: Think about how shame might affect asking for support.

b.q: Two rival school teams in Geelong join to build one community garden, sharing the planning equally. Which feature is most likely to reduce prejudice between them?
opts: A shared goal pursued on equal terms
Hearing a teacher lecture about the other team
Competing to see which team wins a prize
Meeting only briefly, with one team in charge
b.why: Working together toward one goal, with neither team in charge, fits both shared goals and equal terms. Competition and unequal status can keep or increase prejudice, and a lecture alone does not give contact.
b.clue: Look for the option that has both cooperation and equal status.

a.best: It can isolate them and stop them seeking help

b.best: A shared goal pursued on equal terms

proposal.title: Stigma and reducing prejudice
card: a mark of shame that society attaches to a person or group, such as for a mental illness. Stigma can lead people to be avoided or judged.
Prejudice, discrimination and stigma can harm wellbeing. They can cause stress, isolation and lower self-esteem, and can stop people seeking help.
Contact between groups can reduce prejudice when it is on equal terms, with neither group holding more status or power. Working toward a shared goal that needs everyone helps too.

a.q: Lena has an anxiety disorder. She avoids seeing a doctor because she fears her classmates will judge her. How is stigma affecting her wellbeing?
opts: It is stopping her from getting the help that she needs
It is lowering her stress by keeping her problem private
It is protecting her self-esteem from others' judgement
It is reducing her isolation by keeping her problem hidden
a.why: Fear of being judged is keeping Lena from treatment, which is one way stigma harms wellbeing. Hiding a problem can seem to lower stress or protect self-esteem, but stigma tends to raise stress, lower self-esteem and increase isolation.
a.clue: Think about what fear of being judged makes people avoid.

b.q: A Geelong school wants to reduce prejudice between students from its two rival campuses. Which plan best meets both conditions for contact to reduce prejudice?
opts: Mixed teams paint one mural, each student with an equal say
Mixed teams paint one mural, led by students from one campus
Each campus paints a mural, and the better one wins a prize
Both campuses sit together at assembly, with no shared task
b.why: One mural that needs everyone, with an equal say for all, gives a shared goal on equal terms. The plan led by one campus has a shared goal but gives one group more power, so it misses equal status. The contest and the assembly give no goal that needs both groups.
b.clue: Ask what each plan leaves out.
